import BuildAppPipeline from '../../../components/diagrams/BuildAppPipeline.astro';

Once your app compiles, it still has to become something a node can install.
That deliverable is an **`.mpk` bundle**: a single archive carrying your
`calimero:app` component, a `manifest.json`, and an Ed25519 signature.
This page walks the builder workflow that produces one.

The signing tool is `mero-sign` (`tools/mero-sign/`); `scripts/pack-component.py`
writes the manifest, signs it through `mero-sign` and packs the archive. The node
side — how a bundle is parsed, verified, and trusted on install — lives in
[Upgrades & migration](/protocol/upgrades/); this page does not duplicate that
detail.

<BuildAppPipeline />

## The workflow

<Steps>

1. **Build the component.**

   `calimero-app-build` compiles your crate for `wasm32-wasip2` and turns it into a
   `calimero:app` component, with the ABI the SDK's macros embed (its
   `calimero:abi` section):

   ```bash
   scripts/install-mero-app-build.sh   # once: puts mero-app-build on PATH
   mero-app-build apps/my-app --out my-app.wasm
   ```

   A WASM core module (an SDK 0.12 app) is refused by the node
   (`400 UNSUPPORTED_BUNDLE`).

2. **Generate a signing key (one-time).**

   `mero-sign generate-key` creates an Ed25519 keypair and derives your **signer
   id** — a `did:key` identifier built from the public key (the `0xed01`
   ed25519-pub multicodec tag plus the 32-byte key, base58btc-encoded under the
   `did:key:` prefix).

   ```bash
   mero-sign generate-key --output my-signing-key.json
   # Generated new keypair: my-signing-key.json
   #   signerId: did:key:z6Mkrb81NKkv7Mw4dZAWA5PTuwBhbq9u9eCPuby3icBUdirg
   ```

   The key file is JSON with base64url-encoded `privateKey` and `publicKey` plus
   the derived `signerId` (`mero-sign derive-signer-id --key <file>` prints it
   again). `generate-key` will not overwrite an existing file unless you pass
   `--force`, which loses the old key for good. **Keep it secret and out of version control** — it is
   your update authority (see below).

   <Aside type="caution">
   For local development you can sign with the built-in well-known dev key via
   `mero-sign sign <manifest> --dev` instead of `--key`. A dev-signed bundle is
   marked as such, **cannot be published to the registry**, and is refused
   (`403 DEV_SIGNED_PACKAGE`) by a node not running with `--dev` or
   `--allow-unsigned-bundles` — use a generated key for anything real.
   </Aside>

3. **Write and sign the manifest, and create the `.mpk`.**

   `scripts/pack-component.py` writes `manifest.json` (`version`, `package`,
   `appVersion`, `minRuntimeVersion` and the `app.wasm` artifact with its SHA-256
   and size), has `mero-sign sign` sign it, and packs `manifest.json` and
   `app.wasm` into a gzip-compressed tar. `mero-sign` derives the `signerId` from
   the key, refuses to sign if `minRuntimeVersion` is absent (a signer must not
   rewrite the document it signs), canonicalizes the manifest with RFC 8785 (JCS),
   signs the domain-tagged SHA-256 of those canonical bytes, and writes a
   `signature` object back into the manifest.

   ```bash
   python3 -I scripts/pack-component.py --wasm my-app.wasm --package com.example.my-app \
     --app-version 1.0.0 --key my-signing-key.json --out dist/com.example.my-app-1.0.0.mpk
   # omit --key to sign with the development key
   ```

   The script runs from a checkout of core: it signs through `cargo run -p
   mero-sign` unless `--mero-sign` (or `MERO_SIGN`) names a `mero-sign`
   binary. `--min-runtime-version` (default `0.1.0`) is the oldest `merod`
   release the app needs; a cluster with an older replica refuses the upgrade
   (`409 RUNTIME_TOO_OLD`). For every release after the first, pass
   `--previous <last .mpk>`: `mero-sign` then compares the two ABIs, warns about
   changes that break callers, and refuses a state change made without a state
   version bump ([App interface](/build/app-abi/#check-a-new-version-against-the-last)).

   <Aside type="caution">
   The manifest has fields the script does not write: `outbound` (the URL
   prefixes a run may call, [Call an external service](/build/guides/outbound/)),
   `upgrades` (`owner`, the default, or `publisher`), `frontend`, `links` and
   multi-service `services` (`calimero_bundle::BundleManifest`). A release that
   needs them is packed by a tool that writes them before `mero-sign sign
   manifest.json --key <file>`; check the one you use.
   </Aside>

   An app with compute methods also builds a compute component
   (`mero-app-build <crate> --out app.wasm --compute-out compute.wasm`). Pass it
   with `--compute compute.wasm`: the manifest then declares it as `compute`, and
   the `.mpk` carries it as `compute.wasm`. Without it a release cannot run
   compute, and neither can a raw `.wasm` upload. `--compute` without `--wasm`
   packs a package with only a compute component.

   A release may also ship pipelines over its compute methods: `--pipeline
   daily.yaml` (repeatable) packs each file as `pipelines/<name>`, and the
   manifest lists it under `pipelines` (at most 16 per package, each at most
   64 KiB), signed with the rest. The node compiles each file at install and
   checks it against the package's own compute methods and the cluster's pools:
   the module is `self` (or left out) or another installed package by its exact
   name, optionally pinned (`module: com.acme.pdf@0.1.0`; without a version, the
   newest release the installer sees). That package must ship a compute component;
   its methods and caps are the ones the step is checked against, a module the
   installer cannot see or that has none is `UNKNOWN_MODULE`, and the release
   keeps running the module release it was installed against until the pipeline's
   own package is released again. The module's package cannot be uninstalled while
   such a release exists (`409 MODULE_IN_USE`). The step's files, payer and usage
   stay the calling app's. Every method must be one its module
   declares, and each step's limits may only lower the method's caps. A problem
   is `400 BAD_PIPELINE` with `details`, a list of `{file, path, code, message}`
   for every error. A release with pipelines installs only once every node runs
   this release (`409 CLUSTER_NOT_UPGRADED`). `meroctl app pipelines PACKAGE`
   prints what a version registered.

4. **Install it.**

   A real cluster installs releases from its operator's registry
   (`POST /packages/install { package, version }`); publish the `.mpk` there.
   A development cluster (`merod --dev`, and `merod local`) also takes an
   upload:

   ```bash
   meroctl app install --path dist/com.example.my-app-1.0.0.mpk
   meroctl context create --name my-app --package com.example.my-app --alias my-app
   ```

   Before it logs the install, the node checks the publisher's signature and
   every artifact's digest, `minRuntimeVersion`, the package's pinned signer
   (the first release's), and that each component prepares and imports only
   what the `calimero:app` world offers. Installing is what *produces* an
   application: the manifest's `package` and `signerId` fix the application id.
   A WASM that a release of another signer's package already ships is refused
   (`409`).

</Steps>

## The signer key is the update authority

For a bundle, the application id is derived from the `package` **and** the
`signerId` together — not from the bytecode. That makes the application id
**version-stable**: a new release signed by the *same* key under the *same*
package keeps the same application id and is recognized as an upgrade of the
existing app.

The corollary is the rule to remember: **a new signed version must use the same
signer key.** Sign a new release with a different key and the node computes a
different application id — it is a *different application*, not an upgrade, and
existing contexts will not pick it up. Treat the signing key as the long-lived
identity of your app and guard it accordingly.

<Aside type="note" title="Every install path requires a signature">
There is one rule, not a per-path split: a bundle must carry a valid Ed25519
manifest signature to be installed, whether it comes from a registry, a URL, or
a local file. Dev builds are not an exception - they sign with the well-known
dev key (`mero-sign sign --dev`) and are verified like any other bundle; since
that key's seed is public, only a development node (`--dev` or
`--allow-unsigned-bundles`) installs a release it signed. The
signature also binds the wasm bytes: each wasm artifact is checked against the
SHA-256 the signed manifest records for it. The exact verification rules are
documented in [Upgrades & migration](/protocol/upgrades/).
</Aside>
